title: Naming and praising the Lord of all worlds
tafsir:
These four ayat open the Qur'an, and they are pure praise: the Name of Allah is invoked, then He is praised as Nurturer of every world, as the One whose mercy is boundless and perfect, and as Master of the Day when everything is settled. One movement holds them together — you begin *in His Name*, and having named Him you cannot help but describe Him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out the surah's architecture: of its seven verses, the first three praise Allah, the last three are a request Allah Himself taught us to make, and the verse between carries both. This passage is that opening block of praise.

## The surah being opened

Ibn Kathir gathers its names: **al-Fatihah**, the Opener of the Book, the surah with which prayers are begun; **Umm al-Kitab**, the Mother of the Book, according to the majority of the scholars — al-Bukhari explains the title by saying the Qur'an starts with it and the prayer is started by reciting it, while others say it is because it contains the meanings of the entire Qur'an; and al-Hamd (the Praise), as-Salah (the Prayer, since reciting it is a condition for the prayer's correctness), ash-Shifa' (the Cure) and ar-Ruqyah (the remedy — from the narration of Abu Saʿid about the Companion who used al-Fatihah to heal a poisoned tribal chief). It was revealed in Makkah, as Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah and Abu al-ʿAliyah stated, and there is no disagreement that it contains seven ayat. Imam Ahmad records in the Musnad that the Prophet ﷺ told Abu Saʿid bin al-Muʿalla, "I will teach you the greatest surah in the Qur'an before you leave the Masjid," and taught him this surah; al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, An-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah also record it.

## Ayah 1: beginning with the Name

Before Islam, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, people began everything they did with the names of their idols. It was to uproot that practice that the first verse of the Qur'an brought down to the Prophet ﷺ commanded him to begin with the name of Allah: *Iqra' bismi Rabbik*, "Read with the name of your Lord."

**The letter Ba.** *Bismillah* is composed of three elements: the letter *Ba*, *ism* (name), and *Allah*. The *Ba* carries several senses in Arabic, three of which fit here and all of which apply: contiguity — with the name of Allah; seeking aid — with the help of His name; and seeking blessing — with its barakah. The phrase stays incomplete until one mentions the work being begun, so grammar supplies a verb — "I begin," "I recite" — and propriety places that verb *after* the phrase, so that one actually begins with the Name and nothing precedes it. Arabic does require the *Ba* to stand before the Name; but the ʿUthmani manuscript, prepared under the third Caliph ʿUthman with the consensus of the Companions, made a modification: it dropped the alif and joined the *Ba* to the *Sin*, so the *Ba* looks like part of the word *ism* — and this is peculiar to *Bismillah*, since in *Iqra' bismi Rabbik* the alif is written alongside the *Ba*. The script itself guards the precedence of the Name.

**Allah** is the greatest and most comprehensive of the divine names; according to some scholars it is *al-Ism al-Aʿzam*, the Great Name, though reports differ as to what that Name is. It refers to the Essence, and so it cannot be given to anyone except Allah — which is why the word has neither dual nor plural: Allah is One and has no associate. It is the name of that Ultimate Reality which comprehends every attribute of perfection, creator and sustainer, unique and peerless.

**Is it part of the surah?** All Muslims agree that *Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim* is a verse of the Qur'an, being part of a verse in Surat al-Naml, and agree that it is written at the head of every surah except Surat al-Tawbah. There is, however, a difference of opinion among the *Mujtahids* — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān glosses them as the authentic scholars who are entitled to express an opinion in such matters — as to whether this verse is an integral part of Surat al-Fatihah, or of all the surahs, or of neither. Ibn Kathir reports that according to the majority of the reciters of Kufah, a group of the Companions, the Tabiʿin (the generation of scholars that followed the Companions) and a number of scholars of the successive generations, the *Bismillah* is a separate ayah at al-Fatihah's beginning. Imam Abu Hanifah held that it is not an integral part of any surah except al-Naml; rather it is in itself an independent verse of the Qur'an, revealed to be placed at the head of every surah in order to separate and distinguish one surah from another.

**What it does to a life.** The Qur'an and the ahadith repeatedly direct us to recite it when taking food, drinking water, performing wudu (ablution), and getting on or off a carriage; another narration mentions closing the door of one's house, putting out the lamp, and covering a vessel. The Prophet ﷺ said that no important work receives the blessings of Allah unless it is begun with His name. By instructing man to begin everything this way, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, Islam gives his whole life an orientation towards Allah, so that his ordinary economic and worldly activities become acts of worship. A disbeliever eats and drinks just as a Muslim does; but the Muslim, saying *Bismillah*, affirms that it was never in his power to obtain this little morsel — which passed from the sowing of the seed to the reaping of the grain, requiring the labours of wind, rain and sun, of the heavens and the earth, and of a thousand men — and that Allah alone granted it to him.

## Ayat 2–3: praise, lordship, mercy

*Al-hamdu lillah* signifies that all praise essentially belongs to Allah. Whoever praises anything anywhere in the world is ultimately praising Him: the sensible world contains millions of things that compel our admiration for their beauty and usefulness, but look behind the veil of appearances and each one is the manifestation of the same creative power. Admiring anything created is no more than admiring a work of art or craft, which is in fact praise of the artist or craftsman. So although the phrase is worded as praise, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes, by implication it cuts the very root of worshipping created beings and brings out the first and basic principle of the Islamic creed — that Allah is One.

**Rabb** lexically signifies "one who nurtures," and nurture implies developing a thing by gradual stages, in a manner conducive to its own good, until it attains perfection. The word is exclusive to Allah and cannot be used of a created being without qualification, since a creature itself stands in need of nurture and can nurture no one else. **Al-ʿalamin** is the plural of *ʿalam* (world, universe, kingdom), taking in every possible form of existence: sky and earth, sun, moon and stars, wind and rain, the angels, the jinn, animals, plants, minerals, and of course men. It is reported from the Companion Abu Saʿid al-Khudri that there are forty thousand worlds, ours — stretching from East to West — being only one of them; according to the well-known commentator Muqatil, the number is eighty thousand. Imam Razi held that Allah, being All-Powerful, could well have created millions of other universes in the space beyond our own.

Seen in this light, the universe reveals itself as an incredibly complex yet perfectly integrated order, in which everything from the heavens to the particles of dust performs the function assigned to it by Divine Wisdom. Man cannot obtain a morsel of food unless a thousand forces of sky and earth work together to produce it; and if Allah has put millions of His creatures in man's service, then man in his turn cannot be worthless or purposeless. The Qur'an is insistent that the universe is not absurd — the heavens and the earth were not created in vain (38:27) — and it states the purpose of man's own existence: "I have not created the jinn and mankind except to worship Me" (51:56). So *Rabb al-ʿalamin* is in a way the proof of *al-hamdu lillah*: when Allah alone is the ultimate cause of the nurture of the whole universe, He alone can in reality be worthy of praise.

Ayah 3 names two of the Beautiful Names, both from the root *rahmah* (mercy), indicating the all-pervasiveness and perfection of divine mercy. **Ar-Rahman** signifies one whose mercy is common to all and extends to the whole universe, to everything that will be created in the future; it is Allah's exclusive attribute, has no dual or plural, and it is not permissible to describe any created being by it, since no one besides Allah can have mercy that is all-embracing — hence Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's ruling that those who shorten a name such as ʿAbd al-Rahman or Fadl al-Rahman into "Rahman" are doing what is not permissible. **Ar-Rahim** signifies mercy perfect in all possible ways, and since its meaning contains nothing impossible to find in a creature — a man may be perfectly merciful in his dealings with another — it may justifiably be used of a human being, as the Qur'an itself uses it of the Prophet ﷺ. The mention of mercy at just this point, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān suggests, is perhaps meant to remind us that it was not through any external compulsion or inner need that Allah assumed the responsibility of nurturing His whole creation, but in response to the demand of His own quality of mercy. Had this universe not existed He would suffer no loss; that it does exist is no burden to Him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes Rumi here: there was nothing, neither our being nor our claim to be — it was Thy mercy that heard our unsaid.

## Ayah 4: Master of the Day of Judgment

*Malik* is derived from the root *milk*: possessing a thing in such a manner that one has the right and power to dispose of it as one likes. *Din* signifies requital. No object of that mastery is named; according to the commentary al-Kashshaf the phrase makes a general reference covering everything — on the Day of Requital, mastery over everything that exists will belong to Allah alone.

**What is the Day of Requital?** It is the Day appointed by Allah to recompense good or evil deeds. This world is only the field of action, the place where one performs one's duty, not the place for receiving one's reward. That a man happens to be healthy, wealthy or powerful does not argue that he has won Allah's pleasure, nor does illness, poverty or weakness by itself indicate that he is the object of Allah's wrath — which is why the greatest sufferings in this world are the lot of the Prophets and, after them, of the men of Allah, whom we nevertheless see content and even happy. A man may receive some punishment or reward for his deeds here, but this is never the full recompense; only a faint model, manifested as an intimation or warning (32:21; 68:33). Given that good and evil are not equal in value, justice requires a world beyond this one where every deed, big or small, is judged and then justly repaid — what the Qur'an calls al-Akhirah (the world to come), al-Qiyamah (the Day of Judgment), and *Yawm al-Din* (the Day of Requital): "The hour of retribution is sure to come, no doubt about it, yet most people do not believe" (40:58–59).

**Why name that Day, when Allah is Master now?** The real master of every particle of dust can only be He who created and nurtured it, whose mastery has neither beginning nor end and covers the living and the dead, the apparent and the hidden, the seen and the unseen. Man's mastery, by contrast, is bounded at both ends — there was a "before" when it did not exist and there will be an "after" when it exists no more — and it reaches only the living, the seen, the external aspect of things. So the real Master, not only on the Day of Requital but even now, is Allah. Yet Allah in His beneficence has granted man a kind of imperfect, temporary and apparent mastery as well, and Islamic law, in laying down rules for worldly affairs, gives due consideration to man's limited right of ownership; and man, handed lands and money and power by way of trial, has always been prone to get drunk with pride and vanity. So this ayah is a warning to man reeling in his forgetfulness and self-conceit: all he possesses is short-lived, and a Day is coming when masters will no more be masters and slaves no more slaves, when no one will own anything even in appearance, and the ownership of the whole universe, apparent as well as real, will be seen to belong to none but Allah — "'Whose is the kingdom today?' Of Allah alone, the One, the Mighty" (40:17).

## What Allah says back

Ibn Kathir cites Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, who heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say that Allah, the Exalted, said: "I have divided the prayer into two halves between Myself and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same hadith from the Sahih of Muslim on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, and gives it in fuller form. In its rendering, when the servant says *al-hamdu lillahi Rabbil-ʿalamin*, Allah says, "My servant has paid his homage to Me"; when he says *ar-Rahman ar-Rahim*, Allah says, "My servant has praised Me"; and when he says *Maliki Yawmid-Din*, Allah says, "My servant has proclaimed My greatness." (Ibn Kathir narrates this same hadith in full at a later ayah of the surah, with slightly different wording in translation.)

In every prayer, then, you name Allah, praise Him for nurturing every world, take shelter in a mercy that owed you nothing, and hand over the Day you cannot control — and each sentence is answered.
